episode.project: A from-scratch museum exhibit label assembly pipeline: a small module that cleans title/tag tokens and gradually assembles wall-label text lines and gallery index lines from JSON exhibit records, under evolving house conventions for invalid input and token ordering.

source_messages.text: We're building up the museum exhibit label pipeline step by step. This module has one finished helper (_clean_token) and three stub functions we'll grow over the next few edits. Two workstreams: 'wall-labels' for visitor-facing label text, and 'gallery-index' for the index board. I tell you which one each request belongs to.

Project-wide standing rule: whenever you write a new function or edit an existing one, any invalid input must return the string 'ERR'. Never raise exceptions, and never return null for the invalid case. This holds until I say otherwise, and it applies from the moment an edit is made — I never expect you to retro-fix untouched functions when conventions change.

request.text: First real edit, on the wall-labels side: implement label_title(record) in module.py. It takes exactly one JSON value, the exhibit record. The record is valid only if it is an object with a 'name' entry that is a string and that yields at least one clean token when the name is split on whitespace and each piece is passed through _clean_token. For a valid record return the cleaned name tokens, each capitalized, joined with single spaces — so {'name': 'The blue VASE!'} gives 'The Blue Vase'. Every other input (not an object, missing or non-string name, or a name with no cleanable token) is invalid; return the project's invalid-input result. Use _clean_token rather than writing your own cleanup.

rounds.manual_recap: Rules currently binding this edit: (1) Invalid input must return the string 'ERR', never raise — this global rule governs any function being newly written, so label_title must follow it. That is the only standing rule in force right now; there are no ordering conventions and no workstream-specific permissions or exceptions yet.

effective_rules.text: Any function newly written or edited returns the string 'ERR' for invalid input and never raises; untouched earlier functions are never retro-rewritten when conventions change.

source_messages.text: One more project-wide rule before you start the index side: whenever an output presents a sorted list of cleaned tokens, sort by the cleaned token's length, shortest first, and when two cleaned tokens tie on length keep their original input order — a stable sort, explicitly not alphabetical order. This applies to any function you write or edit from now on.

request.text: Now switch workstreams: on the gallery-index side, implement index_entry(record). One JSON argument. Valid only if it is an object with 'number' an integer (booleans do not count) that is >= 0, and 'tags' a list whose elements are all strings. Clean every tag with _clean_token and drop the ones that become empty, then present the survivors sorted under the standing sorted-token convention. Render the number zero-padded to at least three digits (7 -> '007', 3000 -> '3000'). Return 'NNN: t1, t2' with the tokens joined by ', ' — and if no token survives, return just 'NNN' with no colon at all. Any other input shape is invalid; use the project's invalid-input result.

rounds.manual_recap: Rules currently binding this edit (the task switch does not relax anything): (1) Invalid input returns the string 'ERR' — required globally. (2) Any sorted list of cleaned tokens must be sorted by cleaned length ascending, with length ties keeping their original input order (stable, not alphabetical) — required globally, and it applies here because this entry emits a sorted tag-token list. No workstream-specific permissions exist yet.

When an output presents a sorted list of cleaned tokens, sort by cleaned token length ascending; equal lengths keep their original input order (stable sort, not alphabetical). Applies to functions written or edited while in force.

source_messages.text: Quick scope note before this next edit, wall-labels only: in the label functions, for invalid input you MAY return null (None) instead of the otherwise-applicable invalid-input result. This is genuinely optional — the otherwise-applicable result remains fully acceptable and tests accept either. Permission, not a requirement, and it does not carry over to the gallery-index side.

request.text: Staying on wall-labels, implement label_full(record). One JSON argument. Valid only if it satisfies label_title's name requirement AND has 'artist', a string yielding at least one clean token, AND 'year', an integer (not a boolean) greater than 0. For a valid record return a three-element list in this exact order: label_title(record), then 'by ' followed by the capitalized cleaned artist tokens joined with single spaces, then str(year). Example: {'name': 'vase', 'artist': 'ada lovelace', 'year': 1889} -> ['Vase', 'by Ada Lovelace', '1889']. Anything else is invalid and follows the conventions currently in force for this workstream. This function's output is a fixed-order list of label lines, not a sorted token list.

episode.project: A single-channel stage-lighting toolkit using integer time units: run-length compaction of per-channel level samples, greedy non-overlapping scheduling of named cues with requested starts and durations, and an integration step that renders both results together.

source_messages.text: Welcome to the lighting project. module.py holds a tiny validated helper plus three stubs we'll grow into a cue compaction and scheduling pipeline; times and durations are plain integers. Two standing rules for any function you write or edit in this project: 1) Whenever an argument doesn't match the documented valid shape, return exactly the string "invalid" — never null, and never raise. 2) Whenever you have to order items that compare equal on the ordering key, keep the order they first appeared in the input. These rules attach when a function is written or edited; I'll never silently expect you to rewrite earlier working functions when rules evolve.

One open choice, also standing: a compacted run may be represented either as a two-item list [level, count] or as an object {"level": <int>, "count": <int>}. Both are acceptable anywhere runs are produced — pick whichever you prefer; tests accept both.

request.text: Time to fill in compact_cue(payload) in module.py. It takes one argument: a list of light-level samples for one channel, where every sample must be a JSON integer (booleans are not integers here). Compact it into runs of equal consecutive values: return one run per maximal block of equal neighbors, each run recording that block's value and how many samples it contains, with runs in the order they occur. An empty list compacts to an empty list. Anything that isn't a valid sample list counts as invalid input — follow our standing rules for that, and for how runs may be represented. Submit just the new compact_cue definition.

rounds.manual_recap: Currently applicable standing obligations for this edit: (1) Global, required — invalid-input representation: any payload that does not match the documented valid shape (not a list, or any element that is not a JSON integer) must return exactly the string "invalid"; never null, never an error object, never an exception. (2) Global, permitted — run representation: each produced run may be a two-element list [level, count] or an object {"level": ..., "count": ...}; both are always acceptable and neither is mandatory. No task-local override exists. The global first-seen tie rule is live but imposes nothing here, because this function preserves input order and resolves no equal-key ordering.

effective_rules.text: For any function you write or edit in this project, an argument that does not match the documented valid shape must return exactly the string "invalid"; it must not return null or any error object and must not raise.
A compacted run may be returned either as a two-element list [level, count] or as an object {"level": <int>, "count": <int>}; both representations are always acceptable and tests must accept either.

source_messages.text: Same two standing rules and the run-representation choice remain in effect — for the new scheduling function too.

request.text: Please implement schedule_cues(payload). payload is a list of cue objects; each cue must have an "id" (a string), an "at" (an integer >= 0, the requested start time) and a "dur" (an integer >= 1); ignore any extra keys, and booleans never count as integers. All cues share a single channel, so placed cues may not overlap. Place them greedily: consider cues in ascending requested start (resolving any ties the way our standing ordering rules require), and give each cue the earliest integer start that is at least its requested at and at least the end of the cue placed before it; its end is start + dur. Return the placements in placement order as objects {"id": ..., "start": ..., "end": ...}. An empty list schedules to an empty list; malformed payloads follow the standing invalid-input rules. Just the schedule_cues definition, please.

rounds.manual_recap: Currently applicable standing obligations for this edit (task cue-scheduling): (1) Global, required — invalid-input representation: any payload violating the documented shape (not a list, or a cue with a missing/mistyped id, at, or dur) must return exactly the string "invalid". (2) Global, required — ordering ties: cues that share the same requested start time must keep their first-seen input order; no task-local override exists yet, so this global rule governs cue-scheduling here. The run-representation permission does not apply because this function produces no runs.

Whenever a function you write or edit must order items that compare equal on the active ordering key, the tied items must keep the relative order in which they first appeared in the input.

Where it applies, this overrides the global first-seen tie rule; the global rule stays in force everywhere else. It applies from the next scheduling function you write or edit. The invalid-string rule is unchanged.

request.text: Extend schedule_cues(payload) so it also accepts a dictionary form {"cues": <cue list exactly as before>, "gap": <integer >= 0>}. In that form, each cue placed after the first must start at least gap time units after the previously placed cue's end — i.e. it starts at its requested at if that is already at least end-of-previous plus gap, otherwise at the earliest integer start satisfying that. Plain list payloads must behave exactly as they do now (a gap of zero); ignore extra dictionary keys; a dictionary missing either key, or whose gap is not a non-negative integer (booleans are not integers), counts as invalid. Everything else — per-cue validation, the tie behavior required by the current standing rules, invalid-input handling — stays governed as before. Give me the full new schedule_cues definition.

episode.project: Puzzle tournament score aggregation and display pipeline: a finished helper assigns base points by finishing place; per-competitor totals are aggregated with optional bonuses and dropped low rounds; leaderboard rows are validated and ranked; a summary formatter produces numbered display lines and, for raw entries, an adopted champion field.

source_messages.text: One standing note before we touch this puzzle-tournament module: whenever you write a new function here or revise an existing one, make a malformed argument come back as JSON null (None) — never raise and never guess a value. That obligation binds only the function you are writing or editing at the time; anything already finished stays exactly as it is, and a later convention change will never silently oblige you to revisit completed code.

request.text: Let's start the scoring side of the tool. Implement solve_total(entry). The argument must be a dict describing one competitor's event: "places" is a list of finishing places (positive integers, 1 = first place), and "bonus" is an optional non-negative integer of extra points that defaults to 0 when absent. Extra keys are fine — ignore them. Booleans do not count as integers anywhere here. The result is the sum of base_points(p) for every listed place, plus the bonus. Anything that does not match this shape is malformed and should follow our standing convention.

The argument must be a list of rows, where each row is a dict with "name" (a non-empty string) and "total" (an integer, which may be negative; booleans do not count). Names must be unique — a repeated name makes the whole input malformed, as does anything else that fails this shape. Return a new list of {"name": ..., "total": ...} dicts ordered by total from highest to lowest. Tie-handling rule for this task: rows with equal totals are ordered alphabetically by name, A to Z, meaning case-sensitive Python string lexicographic ordering by Unicode code points — no locale sorting and no case-folding. An empty list is valid input and returns an empty list.

episode.project: A fictional seedling-tray slot allocator and occupancy-summary pipeline over integer grids. A tray is a map {rows, cols, blocked} of positive grid dimensions and blocked integer cells; an allocator fills batches into free slots, a summarizer reports occupancy of a tray plus placements, and a planner chains several batches and summarizes the combined result. All grid rules are invented for this exercise.

source_messages.text: Kicking off a small project: a fictional seedling-tray allocator in a single file, module.py. It already has a finished helper is_tray and three stubs I will ask you to fill over several turns: assign_slots, summarize_occupancy, plan_report. We track two task handles here: 'allocation' and 'reporting'.

Standing convention for the whole project, applying to any function as you newly write it or later edit it — this is not a request to rewrite functions you have already finished: whenever your function selects among available slots or returns slot coordinates, use reading order — lowest row first, then lowest column — and when several slots are equally eligible the earliest slot in that order wins.

Second standing convention, same write-time/edit-time scope only: when a newly written or edited function receives input that does not match the contract in my request, it answers with exactly the string "INVALID".
One bit of latitude: in any dict you return from code you write from now on, the order of the keys is irrelevant to us — any order is permitted, never required.

request.text: Fill in assign_slots(payload) in module.py (allocation task). payload must be a dict with keys "tray" and "batch"; ignore any extra keys. A valid tray is whatever is_tray accepts. A valid batch is a dict with "bid" (a non-empty string) and "count" (an integer >= 1; for this count field only, Python integer booleans are permitted with False meaning 0 and True meaning 1, still subject to count >= 1). Consider the tray's usable slots — every (row, col) not in its blocked list — and place the batch into the first "count" usable slots in reading order (lowest row, then lowest column); if fewer usable slots than "count" remain, fill all of them. Return a dict {"bid": the batch's bid, "placed": the list of [row, col] pairs in the order they were filled, "unplaced": count minus the number placed}. For any payload not meeting this contract, return the string "INVALID". Submit just the complete function.

(2) REQUIRED, global — slot selection and any returned slot coordinates follow reading order: lowest row, then lowest column, ties to the earliest such slot. (3) PERMITTED, global — dict key order is free. These bind the function as it is written now; nothing obliges rewriting already-finished code.

In dicts returned by newly written or edited functions, key order is free latitude and never a requirement.

No thanks on the checksum — for this summary request only, no extra fields beyond what I specify unless I explicitly ask later; this is not a new durable standing convention. Both standing conventions from kickoff still hold for any function you write or edit. Switching to the reporting task for this turn.

request.text: Implement summarize_occupancy(payload) in module.py (reporting task). payload must be a dict with "tray" (valid per is_tray) and "placed": a list of distinct [row, col] integer pairs, each in bounds and not one of the tray's blocked cells; for these placed coordinates only, Python integer booleans are permitted with False meaning 0 and True meaning 1, subject to the same in-bounds and distinctness rules; ignore extra payload keys. Usable cells are all cells minus the blocked ones; occupied cells are the placed ones. Return a dict with exactly these keys: "filled" (number of placed cells), "open" (usable minus filled), and "first_open" (the first usable, unoccupied cell in reading order — lowest row, then lowest column — or null if none exists). Return the string "INVALID" for anything outside this contract: bad tray, malformed placed entries, wrong types, a placed cell that is blocked, out of bounds, or duplicated. Complete function only.
